page_summary:
In an overcrowded near-future America grappling with chronic unemployment and racial tension, a repair technician discovers that a malfunctioning experimental Jifi-scuttler (an instantaneous transit device) has opened a permanent crack into a parallel Earth, empty of humans and available for settlement. As word of the discovery spreads amid a presidential election in which the first Black candidate, Jim Briskin, campaigns partly on a promise to resettle America's unemployed underclass -- many of them held in cryogenic suspension for years for lack of jobs or housing -- to the newly discovered parallel world, competing factions maneuver to control access to and political credit for the alternate Earth, while the parallel world itself turns out to harbor its own indigenous hominid population, complicating the resettlement plan's premise of an empty world available for the taking.

**Why it matters.** The Crack in Space, expanded from Dick's 1964 novella Cantata 140, is notable for its direct engagement with contemporary American racial politics through Jim Briskin's historic candidacy, years before a Black presidential candidacy became a mainstream political possibility in reality. Its parallel-world resettlement plot, complicated by the discovery of an indigenous population the human characters had assumed did not exist, functions as a pointed science-fictional allegory for the colonial premise that supposedly empty land is available for the taking, undercutting the technological-solution optimism of its own premise with an ethical complication its characters did not anticipate.

*The discovery of the parallel Earth's indigenous population leaves the resettlement plan's moral and political legitimacy as unresolved as the overcrowding crisis it was meant to solve.*
